# Judging code with typed questions in Jev

Ask one model twelve questions about one patch and get calibrated probabilities back instead of prose. Rank six requirements, compare five guardrail engines with a Choice, grade a proposed requirement with a Score, and watch the wording of a criterion move every number.

**[▶ Take this lab on the Zenable Learning Hub](https://www.zenable.app/learn?lab=jev-primitives&utm_source=github&utm_medium=labs_repo&utm_campaign=jev-primitives_readme)** — fully hosted sandbox environment, progress tracking, and a full-featured lab workspace.

Eligible paid Zenable customers get an OpenRouter key automatically in their sandbox. Take the hosted version of this lab, with the key already configured, at https://www.zenable.app/learn?lab=jev-primitives&utm_source=github&utm_medium=labs_repo&utm_campaign=jev-primitives_readme.

**Duration** 60 minutes · **Difficulty** Intermediate

**Topics** `Guardrails & Policy` · `Software Development` · `How LLMs Work`

**Prerequisites**

- Comfort reading Python and a shell prompt
- A rough idea of what an automated pull request review does
- A TypeSafe or OpenRouter key, or the recorded answers this rig ships

## Set up AI inference

Your sandbox has no hosted AI key. Automatic keys require an eligible paid plan and an available inference budget. Choose your own OpenRouter key, or use the local model and the lab's recorded-answer steps.

### Option A: use your own OpenRouter key

Create a key at [openrouter.ai/keys](https://openrouter.ai/keys). Then run this in the sandbox terminal, with your key in place of `sk-or-...`:

```bash
zenable-configure-inference sk-or-...
```

The command writes your key and the model settings into `~/.env` and configures every coding agent installed on the sandbox. Open a new terminal so your shell picks them up.

> [!WARNING]
> Your key goes in `~/.env`, never in the lab directory. Every attendee in the sandbox network can read the lab remote, and a key committed there is a key you've shared.

### Option B: use local Ollama (no key)

The sandbox runs [Ollama](https://ollama.com/) with a small model, `qwen3-nothink`, already downloaded and built. Point every agent at it:

```bash
zenable-configure-inference --ollama
```

Then open a new terminal. The model runs on the sandbox's CPU, so expect slower and weaker answers than a hosted model gives you. This option configures coding agents only. For steps that call Jev directly, follow the lab's recorded-answer instructions, such as adding `--fixtures` where shown. Those commands do not switch to recordings automatically.

<details>
<summary>Not on a Zenable sandbox?</summary>

For Option B, install Ollama from [ollama.com/download](https://ollama.com/download). `qwen3:1.7b` is a reasoning model, and thinking makes it very slow on a CPU, so the steps below build a copy with thinking turned off.

Download the model. Run this on its own and wait for it to finish, because the progress display takes over the terminal and swallows anything you paste behind it:

```bash
ollama pull qwen3:1.7b
```

Then build a copy of it with thinking pinned off. It reuses the weights already on disk, so there's no download and it finishes in about a second:

```bash
ollama show --modelfile qwen3:1.7b > Modelfile.nothink
sed -i 's|^FROM /.*|FROM qwen3:1.7b|' Modelfile.nothink
sed -i 's|{{- if and $.IsThinkSet (eq $i $lastUserIdx) }}|{{- if (eq $i $lastUserIdx) }}|' Modelfile.nothink
sed -i 's|{{- if $.Think -}}|{{- if false -}}|' Modelfile.nothink
sed -i 's|{{ if and $.IsThinkSet (not $.Think) -}}|{{ if true -}}|' Modelfile.nothink
grep -q '{{ if true -}}' Modelfile.nothink
ollama create qwen3-nothink -f Modelfile.nothink
```

Then set the variables below in your environment, for example in a `~/.env` file that your shell loads with `set -a; . ~/.env; set +a`. Claude Code reads the `ANTHROPIC_*` variables, and agents that speak the OpenAI API, such as Codex, read `OPENAI_BASE_URL` and `OPENAI_API_KEY`.

## Getting started

_~7 min · Hands-on_

Let's get the rig down and installed:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Zenable-io/labs.git ~/zenable-labs 2>/dev/null \
  || git -C ~/zenable-labs pull --ff-only
cd ~/zenable-labs/labs/jev-primitives
uv sync --locked
```

Now the credential. The rig reads `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` and `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL` from `~/.env`, the file every new terminal exports. On a Zenable sandbox the hosted key is already there; anywhere else, the setup section at the top of this lab covers it.

The rig reads that file on every command rather than once per shell, so a key that arrives halfway through this lab takes effect on the very next line you run, in the terminal you already have.

If you haven't got a key, add `--fixtures` to the end of every command from here on.

Let's ask Jev something:

```bash
uv run python -m jevlab ask
```

```console
{
  "changes_an_amount": {
    "noul": 0.95,
    "type": "noul"
  },
  "is_python": {
    "noul": 0.99,
    "type": "noul"
  }
}
```

Success! Two questions, one request, one state, and two probabilities back. `is_python` and `changes_an_amount` are names we picked; Jev never saw either of them, and the answers arrived under the keys we sent.

A Noul returns the number and nothing else, so there's no prose to parse and nothing to fall back on when the parse fails.

## Ranking six requirements against one patch

_~13 min · Hands-on_

The rig carries a small change to a refunds module, plus six of the rules a payments team might write down. Here are two of the six, from `jevlab/subjects.py`:

```python
Requirement(
    name="money-as-minor-units",
    statement=(
        "Monetary amounts are carried as integer minor units or as Decimal. "
        "A float never holds an amount of money."
    ),
    rationale="Binary floating point cannot represent most decimal amounts exactly.",
),
Requirement(
    name="docs-links-carry-utm",
    statement=(
        "A link to the documentation site carries UTM parameters naming the "
        "surface the reader clicked from."
    ),
    rationale="Untagged links make it impossible to tell which surface sends readers.",
),
```

The patch adds a clamp on the refund amount and a retry loop around the gateway call.

One of those two requirements has something to say about it and one of them has nothing to say at all, and a reviewer bot has to work out which is which before it spends a token on either.

We ask two Nouls per requirement. Does this rule govern code of the kind these lines touch, and do these lines break it? Twelve questions, one state, one request:

```bash
uv run python -m jevlab rank
```

```console
anchor: patch
rank  requirement                   governs  breaks
   1* retries-carry-idempotency        0.96    0.94
   2* money-as-minor-units             0.95    0.70
   3* structured-logs                  0.94    0.55
   4  jsonb-not-json                   0.13    0.04
   5  no-literal-credentials           0.09    0.04
   6  docs-links-carry-utm             0.03    0.04

top 3 by rank: retries-carry-idempotency, money-as-minor-units, structured-logs
a 0.50 floor on `governs` would have kept 3 of 6
```

The three rules about money, retries and logging sit at the top, and the three about databases, secrets and marketing links sit at the bottom with a clear space between them.

On this file a threshold and a rank agree, and the last line says so.

On a file where they disagree, we'd reach for the rank, because its cost is bounded. It keeps three requirements whatever the numbers do, while a floor keeps everything above it and your bill follows.

Now let's change the question and leave everything else exactly where it is. These two strings live next to each other in `jevlab/questions.py`:

```python
_GOVERNS_BY_PATCH = (
    "Does `requirements.{name}.statement` govern code of the kind the changed "
    "lines in `file.patch` touch?"
)

_GOVERNS_BY_FILE = (
    "Does `requirements.{name}.statement` govern code of the kind `file.content` "
    "contains?"
)
```

Same state, same criteria, same six requirements. The only difference is which part of the state the question points at:

```bash
uv run python -m jevlab rank --anchor file
```

```console
anchor: file
rank  requirement                   governs  breaks
   1* money-as-minor-units             0.94    0.65
   2* structured-logs                  0.92    0.56
   3* retries-carry-idempotency        0.90    0.94
   4  no-literal-credentials           0.28    0.04
   5  jsonb-not-json                   0.15    0.04
   6  docs-links-carry-utm             0.04    0.04

top 3 by rank: money-as-minor-units, structured-logs, retries-carry-idempotency
a 0.50 floor on `governs` would have kept 3 of 6
```

The top three reorder, and `no-literal-credentials` climbs several places, because the whole file imports a payment gateway and a store while the changed lines touch neither.

Asking about the file and asking about the change are different questions, and the one you wrote is the one you get an answer to. A reviewer that wants to comment on a diff has to ask about the diff.

Run the same command three times over and watch what moves:

```bash
uv run python -m jevlab rank --repeat 3
```

```console
pass 1: retries-carry-idempotency > money-as-minor-units > structured-logs
pass 2: money-as-minor-units > retries-carry-idempotency > structured-logs
pass 3: retries-carry-idempotency > money-as-minor-units > structured-logs

top 3 set identical on all 3 passes:   True
top 3 order identical on all 3 passes: False

requirement                    governs range   spread
retries-carry-idempotency        0.95-0.96       0.01
money-as-minor-units             0.95-0.95       0.00
structured-logs                  0.91-0.94       0.03
jsonb-not-json                   0.11-0.13       0.02
no-literal-credentials           0.09-0.11       0.02
docs-links-carry-utm             0.03-0.03       0.00
```

Three identical requests, and the top two swapped places on one of them.

Yours may hold all three passes in the same order, because the two requirements at the top are a hundredth of a point apart and which one wins is a coin toss. What held every time is which three survived.

Question: your reviewer bot picks the top three requirements and comments on them. Which of the two lines in that output would you build the bot on, and what would you have to change about the question to make the other one steady too?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

Build on the set. It held across all three passes here, and it's the thing your bot actually consumes, because it comments on three requirements without caring which of them it read first.

The order is steady everywhere the options aren't tied, and no amount of averaging or hysteresis turns a genuine tie into a stable ranking. It turns a tie into a consistent answer, which is a different thing.

If the difference between first and second place matters to you, the criteria have to say what separates them. Reproducibility here is a property of the question you wrote.

</details>

## Asking how much of a requirement each engine can check

_~12 min · Hands-on_

A requirement is more useful when something automated enforces it, so the next question is which of our guardrail engines could carry `money-as-minor-units`. The rig describes five of them by what they can see, then asks one Choice per engine over three options:

```python
CHOICE_OPTIONS: dict[str, str] = {
    "full": (
        "Every condition the requirement states can be expressed as a check this "
        "engine runs. A change that satisfies the check satisfies the requirement."
    ),
    "partial": (
        "Some of what the requirement states can be expressed as a check this "
        "engine runs, and some of it cannot. A change that passes the check may "
        "still break the requirement."
    ),
    "none": (
        "Nothing the requirement states can be expressed as a check this engine "
        "runs, because the engine does not read this kind of file or cannot see "
        "the condition the requirement names."
    ),
}
```

```bash
uv run python -m jevlab engines
```

```console
requirement: money-as-minor-units   shape: one Choice per engine

engine         choice   full  partial   none  include  guidance
semgrep       partial   0.01     0.99   0.00      yes       yes
eslint        partial   0.04     0.95   0.01      yes       yes
checkov          none   0.00     0.04   0.96       no        no
sqlfluff      partial   0.01     0.65   0.34      yes       yes
gitleaks         none   0.00     0.02   0.98       no        no

include when p(full) + p(partial) >= 0.30; guidance when p(partial) > p(full)
```

Three engines are worth generating a guardrail for, and none of the five can carry the whole rule on its own. Look at the last two columns, because they're two decisions read from one distribution.

Whether to include the engine comes from `full` plus `partial`, and whether the generated guardrail needs a warning that it only covers part of the rule comes from `partial` against `full`.

Now let's ask the same thing as a Noul, one probability per engine:

```bash
uv run python -m jevlab engines --shape noul
```

```console
requirement: money-as-minor-units   shape: one Noul per engine

engine       p(can check)
semgrep              0.70
eslint               0.74
checkov              0.05
sqlfluff             0.19
gitleaks             0.03

a 0.30 floor keeps 2 of 5 engines
one number per engine, so nothing here says which of them need help
```

Two things changed. The full and partial axis has gone, so there's nothing left to decide which of the surviving engines needs a warning attached to it.

And `sqlfluff` dropped out entirely, because "can this engine check the rule" is a harder question than "how much of it can this engine check", and a partial answer has nowhere to go.

Question: both shapes were asked about the same five engines with the same state. Why are the Noul numbers and the Choice numbers not comparable, and which of the two would you trust a 0.30 threshold on?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

A Choice normalises across its options, so every probability in a row is relative to the other options in that row.

A Noul is absolute and answers one proposition on its own, and the docs are explicit that several Nouls can all be low for the same subject while a Choice over the same options has to pick a winner.

That makes a threshold calibrated on one meaningless on the other. Here the Choice is the shape to build on, because both decisions we want come out of one distribution, and a Noul would have thrown the second one away before we made it.

</details>

## Grading a proposed requirement against a rubric

_~13 min · Hands-on_

The last primitive grades something along a named axis. Our subject is a proposed requirement somebody wrote in a hurry: "Code should be clean and handle errors properly, and developers should make sure that money is dealt with carefully." We grade it on testability, specificity and scope.

A Score needs an ordered list of levels, and the rig keeps both of its level sets in one short file:

```python
"""Copyright (c) 2026 Zenable, Inc. The level sets a Score is graded against, and where they land on 0 to 10.

Both readings share one anchor tuple and differ only in what their levels
describe. They sit in one short file because the wording is the policy: a
reviewer who wants to know what a 5 means reads this, and an edit here changes
every score the rubric produces.
"""

ANCHORS: tuple[float, ...] = (0.0, 3.0, 5.0, 8.0, 10.0)
"""Where each level sits on the 0 to 10 scale a threshold is written against."""

QUALITY_LEVELS: tuple[str, ...] = (
    "Absent. The subject shows nothing of this dimension.",
    "Weak. Traces of it, not enough for a reviewer to rely on.",
    "Adequate. Present and usable, with gaps a reviewer would note.",
    "Strong. Clearly present, and a reviewer would need no clarification.",
    "Exemplary. The best form of this a reviewer could reasonably see.",
)

RISK_LEVELS: tuple[str, ...] = (
    "None. Nothing here would concern a reviewer.",
    "Low. A reviewer would mention it and move on.",
    "Moderate. A reviewer would ask for a change before approving.",
    "High. A reviewer would block the change on it.",
    "Severe. The most serious form of this a reviewer could see.",
)

READINGS: dict[str, tuple[str, tuple[str, ...]]] = {
    "quality": (
        "Higher levels describe a better subject. Choose the level whose "
        "description the subject matches.",
        QUALITY_LEVELS,
    ),
    "risk": (
        "Higher levels describe more concern for a reviewer. Choose the level "
        "whose description the subject matches.",
        RISK_LEVELS,
    ),
}


def rubric_score(probabilities: dict[int, float]) -> float:
    """The level probabilities re-weighted over the anchors.

    `score` off the wire is a position on the level number line, so a threshold
    written against a 0 to 10 scale has to re-weight it. Reading `score`
    directly is an off-by-scale bug that every type check accepts.
    """
    return sum(ANCHORS[level] * weight for level, weight in probabilities.items())
```

```bash
uv run python -m jevlab grade
```

```console
reading: quality

dimension      position  score 0-10   distribution
testability        0.21        0.60   0:0.80 1:0.20 2:0.00 3:0.00 4:0.00
specificity        0.61        1.83   0:0.39 1:0.61 2:0.00 3:0.00 4:0.00
scope              0.45        1.32   0:0.63 1:0.31 2:0.03 3:0.03 4:0.00

mean of the three 0-10 scores: 1.25
`position` is where the answer sits on the level number line, 0 to 4
`score 0-10` re-weights the same distribution over the anchors
```

The two number columns are worth staring at. `position` is what arrives on the wire, and it's a spot on a line from 0 to the top level, weighted by the probabilities.

`score 0-10` is that same distribution re-weighted over the anchors we chose. Send `position` into a rule written for a 0 to 10 rubric and everything scores near zero, which reads as a strict grader rather than as the scale error it is.

> [!WARNING]
> Different distributions produce the same position. All of the weight on level 1 and half of it on each of levels 0 and 2 both arrive as 1.0, which is why the distribution column is there.

Now change one thing. Same question text, same state, same anchors, and the other level set:

```bash
uv run python -m jevlab grade --reading risk
```

```console
reading: risk

dimension      position  score 0-10   distribution
testability        0.67        1.86   0:0.45 1:0.46 2:0.08 3:0.01 4:0.00
specificity        0.87        2.49   0:0.25 1:0.67 2:0.06 3:0.01 4:0.01
scope              0.90        2.50   0:0.34 1:0.51 2:0.09 3:0.04 4:0.02

mean of the three 0-10 scores: 2.28
`position` is where the answer sits on the level number line, 0 to 4
`score 0-10` re-weights the same distribution over the anchors
```

Every number moved, and twenty-odd lines of level text are the only thing that changed between the two runs.

The TypeSafe docs name the reason: ["Every level is evaluated separately. The model doesn't see a level's number or its neighbours"](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/score), so the wording of a level is the whole of what it means.

Question: the risk run scores higher than the quality run on all three dimensions. Does that mean the risk reading is the more generous grader?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

No, because the two runs asked different questions. One asks how good the statement's testability is, and the other asks how much that testability would worry a reviewer. Those have no shared scale, so comparing their numbers says nothing at all.

The useful habit is to treat a level set and a threshold as one unit.

A cut point calibrated against the quality levels means nothing against the risk levels, and it means nothing against a third set somebody adds next quarter either. Change the levels, recalibrate the threshold.

</details>
